definition.text: The full value people get from a natural resource, heritage site or infrastructure compared with not having it, built up from several kinds of value.

facts.text: In environmental economics it adds up the values that an ecosystem provides.
It splits into use value, direct (removable products such as timber, fish and water) or indirect (non-removable things such as a sunset or waterfall), and non-use value.
Non-use value covers simply knowing a resource exists, such as knowing tigers live in the wild though you may never see one.
Option value is placed on keeping the possibility of using a resource in future, even when future use is unlikely.
Bequest value comes from preserving natural or cultural heritage for future generations.
Cost–benefit analysis uses a similar approach to the environmental analysis of total economic value.

definition.text: The satisfaction people get from preserving natural or cultural heritage for future generations.

facts.text: It is often used when estimating the value of an environmental good or service.
Together with existence value it makes up non-use value.
Ecosystem valuation counts it as the welfare an ecosystem may give future generations.
In some optimization models it is called the 'salvage value' of the system.

definition.text: The benefit people get simply from knowing that something, such as Antarctica, the Grand Canyon or an endangered species, exists.

facts.text: It is a leading example of non-use value, since no direct use of the resource is needed.
John V. Krutilla introduced the idea in his essay 'Conservation Reconsidered', arguing that undisturbed wilderness has economic value.
It is usually measured with contingent valuation surveys.
Since Ohio v. Department of the Interior, existence values can be recovered as damages in US law.
Damages after the Exxon Valdez oil spill included an estimate of the existence value of a pristine Prince William Sound.

definition.text: What people are willing to pay to keep a public asset or service available even if they are unlikely ever to use it.

facts.text: It is used in policy assessment to justify investing in parks, wildlife refuges, land conservation and rail services.
In environmental research it means the value of preserving threatened natural resources so they might be used in future.
Burton Weisbrod developed the idea in 1964, resting it on uncertain future need, irreversible or costly loss, and the asset not being storable.
Later economists proposed refinements such as 'option price' and 'quasi option value', which stresses irreversibility.
It differs from option value in finance, though both can be read as valuing risk.

definition.text: In ethics, the value something has in itself, for its own sake, rather than as a means to something else.

facts.text: It contrasts with instrumental value, which something has because of its relation to another valued thing.
Every major ethical theory treats something as intrinsically valuable, such as flourishing for virtue ethics or pleasure for consequentialists.
Some conservation biologists argue nature has intrinsic value independent of its usefulness to people.
Arne Næss's deep ecology, coined in 1972, gave all non-human beings intrinsic value.
The Zoological Society of London says insect decline means a loss of species' intrinsic value as well as their instrumental value.
Whether absolute intrinsic value exists is debated; John Dewey accepted only value relative to a situation.

definition.text: The philosophical distinction between what is good as a means to an end and what is good as an end in itself.

facts.text: A hammer or washing machine has instrumental value, while happiness and pleasure are usually thought valuable for their own sake.
The sociologist Max Weber coined the terms.
John Dewey thought belief in intrinsic value was a mistake and treated instrumental judgment as the only way to coordinate behavior well.
J. Fagg Foster treated sustainability as a synonym for instrumental value, since success must never be short term.

definition.text: The usefulness of a thing: the features that let it satisfy a human want or need, a concept from classical and Marxist economics.

facts.text: Gold, for example, can serve as money, as decoration or as an excellent electrical conductor.
Adam Smith noted that diamonds have high exchange value but little use, while water is very useful yet cheap.
For Marx, every commodity is both a use value and an exchange value, the proportion in which it trades for other goods.
Turning a use value into a commodity needs preconditions: it must be tradable, ownership must be securely transferable, and there must be real demand.
Marginalist economics later treated use value as coming from the marginal utility consumers find in a good.
Critics of the commodification of nature draw on the Marxian idea that commodities embody both use and exchange value.

title: Anthropocentrism

definition.text: The belief that human beings are the central or most important beings on the planet.

facts.text: From this view humans are separate from and superior to nature, and animals, plants and minerals are resources for human use.
Environmental ethics often treats it as the root cause of human-made problems in the ecosphere.
Its defenders argue that a sound long-term view keeps the environment suitable for humans, and that the real problem is shallow anthropocentrism.
William Grey called for an enriched human-centred idea of human interest to replace short-term, self-regarding views.
Val Plumwood compared its role in green theory to that of androcentrism in feminist theory.
The word 'dominion' in Genesis has been used to justify it, though some now see it as a possible mistranslation.
Pope Francis's 2023 Laudate Deum speaks of a preferable 'situated anthropocentrism'.
J. Howard Moore argued in 1906 that Darwin's theory of common descent 'sealed the doom' of anthropocentrism.

contested_note: Environmental philosophers dispute whether human-centred thinking causes ecological harm or whether only its shallow, short-term form does.

definition.text: The environmental ethic that gives equal inherent value to all living things.

facts.text: It contrasts with anthropocentrism, centred on humans, and sentientism, which values only beings that can feel pleasure or pain; ecocentrism extends value to the whole of nature.
Its four pillars: humans and other species share Earth's community, all species are interdependent, each organism pursues its own good, and humans are not inherently superior.
It includes Albert Schweitzer's 'reverence for life', Peter Singer's animal liberation and Paul W. Taylor's biocentric egalitarianism.
Its advocates often promote biodiversity preservation, animal rights and environmental protection.
Critics call it anti-human and say it focuses too much on individual lives while neglecting wholes such as ecosystems.
The US Endangered Species Act has been described as unusually biocentric for putting non-human species first.

definition.text: The legal recognition of nature as having rights of its own, an application of biocentric values in law.

facts.text: Ecuador was the first country to put rights of nature in its constitution, in 2008.
Its Article 71 gives nature the right to respect for its existence and the regeneration of its life cycles, structure, functions and evolution.
Cities in Maine, Pennsylvania, New Hampshire and Virginia adopted rights-of-nature laws, aimed especially at corporate exploitation and toxic dumping.
It rejects treating nature as a 'resource' to own, use and degrade, as most twentieth-century laws did.

title: Deep ecology

definition.text: An environmental philosophy holding that all living beings have worth regardless of their usefulness to people, and that society should be reshaped to match.

facts.text: Its core principle is that the living environment as a whole has basic moral and legal rights to live and flourish, independent of human use.
Norwegian philosopher Arne Næss first used the phrase in a 1973 article.
Næss contrasted it with 'shallow ecology', which he criticised as utilitarian, human-centred and consumer-oriented.
It rejects the view of nature as a resource to exploit and holds that the materialist paradigm, including the pursuit of economic growth, must be replaced.
Rachel Carson's 1962 Silent Spring is often seen as the start of the movement.
Guha and Martínez Alier argue it ignores overconsumption in the global north, and Murray Bookchin called it misanthropic.
Arguments about the non-market valuation of ecosystems draw on environmental ethics and deep ecology.
Arne Næss coined 'deep ecology' in 1972, arguing that all non-human entities have intrinsic value.

contested_note: Critics call it Eurocentric, misanthropic or unscientific, and deep ecologists dispute each charge.

definition.text: A nature-centred rather than human-centred system of values.

facts.text: It denies any division between humans and the rest of nature that would make humans the only or greater bearers of intrinsic value.
Aldo Leopold conceived the ethic, and his land ethic is central to it.
It values the biotic community as a whole and aims to keep ecosystem composition and processes intact, covering living and non-living systems rather than organisms alone.
Supporters argue that human-centred ethics makes protecting nature always depend on human welfare, while an ecocentric ethic gives it a firmer basis.
Critics argue it risks sacrificing human wellbeing for an ill-defined greater good.

definition.text: A set of values centred on technology, holding that humans can control nature and solve environmental problems through science.

facts.text: Technocentrics accept that environmental problems exist but do not see cutting industry as the solution.
Ecocentrics, by contrast, see themselves as subject to nature and prefer low-impact technology and self-reliance.

definition.text: The branch of philosophy concerned with the natural environment and humans' place in it.

facts.text: It emerged as a branch of philosophy in the 1970s; early figures include Seyyed Hossein Nasr, Richard Routley, Arne Næss and J. Baird Callicott.
A major debate of the 1970s and 80s asked whether nature has value in itself or only instrumental value, with ecocentric and deep ecology views against human-centred ones.
Current issues include environmental activism, environmental justice, climate change and the depletion of finite resources.
Another debate asks whether wilderness really exists or is a cultural construct with colonial overtones, as William Cronon suggested.
Its questions include whether rivers have rights.

definition.text: The ways societies see importance in the non-human world, grouped as extrinsic (instrumental), intrinsic and relational values.

facts.text: Extrinsic values are nature's usefulness to people, such as timber, clean water and air, carbon storage and pollination, often called ecosystem services.
Many extrinsic values can be given an economic value and so enter impact assessments, cost-benefit analyses and national accounts.
Intrinsic values hold that living things and natural systems have worth regardless of any use to humans.
Relational values are the meaningful relationships, responsibilities and cultural connections between people and nature.
IPBES, building on the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, promotes this broad account of nature's values to guide policy and restoration.

definition.text: Murray Bookchin's 1982 philosophy linking how humans treat nature to how they treat each other.

facts.text: It defines nature as a tendency in healthy ecosystems toward more diversity, complementarity and freedom.
Bookchin argued that 'the ecological crisis is a social crisis': practices such as monocropping and overfishing mirror social tendencies to dominate people.
It calls for decentralization, interdependence and direct democracy instead of profit extraction.

definition.text: In political economy, especially Marxian economics, the proportion in which a commodity can be traded for other goods.

facts.text: It is one of four attributes of a commodity, alongside use value, value and price.
For Marx, exchange value is not the same as money price; actual prices only roughly match it.
Marx held that a good's value is set by the socially necessary labour time needed to produce it.
Making something a commodity requires preconditions such as secure, transferable ownership rights, exclusive access and real market demand.
Modern neoclassical economics no longer theorises exchange value separately; it is simply the market price.
Critics of the commodification of nature argue that expressing all kinds of worth through a single exchange value makes things commensurable.

definition.text: The value people place on a good, often a natural resource, even if they never have used it and never will.

facts.text: It is distinguished from use value, which comes from using the good directly.
It can include option value, bequest value, existence value and altruistic value, the value of keeping a resource so that others can use it.
All these categories grew from the idea of option value introduced by Burton Weisbrod in 1964.
Because market prices and other revealed preference methods generally cannot measure it, stated preference surveys such as contingent valuation are used.
Ecosystem valuation sorts the value of ecosystem services into use and non-use categories.

definition.text: The puzzle, also called the diamond–water paradox, that water is far more useful for survival than diamonds, yet diamonds cost much more.

facts.text: Adam Smith is its classic presenter, though it appears as early as Plato's Euthydemus.
Smith separated 'value in use' from 'value in exchange', noting that the most useful things often have little exchange value.
Labor theory of value supporters resolve it by saying price reflects the toil of acquiring a good.
Marginalists resolve it by distinguishing total from marginal utility: water is so plentiful that one more unit adds little, while scarce diamonds add more.
Böhm-Bawerk's farmer with five sacks of grain values the last sack by its least important use, feeding pigeons.
A person dying of thirst in a desert would pay more for water than for diamonds.
Adam Smith is the classic presenter of the paradox, though it appeared as early as Plato.
Smith contrasted value in use with value in exchange: nothing is more useful than water, yet it buys scarcely anything.

definition.text: The split of use value into direct use, from goods taken from nature, and indirect use, from benefits nature provides without anything being removed.

facts.text: Direct use value comes from removable products such as timber, fish and water; indirect use value from things like a sunset or waterfall.
In ecosystem valuation, indirect use value comes through the positive externalities ecosystems provide.
For livestock breeds, direct use value is milk or meat, while indirect use value includes regulating services such as nutrient cycling, seed dispersal and fire control.
Use and indirect use values can often be inferred from behaviour, such as recreational trip costs or hedonic pricing.

sources.title: Animal genetic resources for food and agriculture

definition.text: Values arising from the meaningful relationships, responsibilities and cultural connections between people and nature.

facts.text: They sit alongside intrinsic values, held for their own sake, and extrinsic values, held as means, in one framing of nature's values.
Western regenerative agriculture has been criticised for ignoring the relational values of Indigenous systems, causing epistemic injustice.

definition.text: Goods that are not bought and sold in markets, such as most environmental goods: clean air, clean water, landscapes, parks, rivers and forests.

facts.text: Quantifying their value is inherently uncertain.
Contingent valuation surveys were first proposed by S.V. Ciriacy-Wantrup in 1947 to value a non-market good.
Environmental assets are usually left out of measures of wealth, partly because non-market goods are hard to value.
